newsitem.title: USA: Miami awaits autumn growth, rates ease slightly.
newsitem.headline: Miami awaits autumn growth, rates ease slightly.

text.p: Hurricane Hortense played havoc with air cargo schedules last week, but no serious problems were reported as Miami carriers and forwarders begin heading into their busy fall season.
Cargo rates eased slightly from a few weeks earlier as extra capacity continued due to extra flights for holiday travellers and cargo continued to be light but steady, executives said.
But, as elsewhere around the world, Miami airlines and forwarders were forecasting cargo rates will go up if fuel prices continue high as a result of market jitters over American bombing of Iraq.
"So far we haven't seen any increases," said one forwarder, "but a couple carriers are advising us there may be fuel surcharges."
"We have not passed it on yet," said an executive at one Miami all-cargo carrier, "nobody wants to be first. We're eating the increase right now."
On Friday night, U.S. spot jet fuel prices feel sharply as the fuel market relaxed amid reports Iraq had pledged to suspend military action.

Besides the fuel increases, Miami cargo executives are keeping their eyes on the weather. Hurricane Hortense hit Puerto Rico on Monday September 9 causing flight cancellations and 12 to 24 hour delays for passenger and cargo carriers.

Although the human suffering from these natural disasters is great, hurricane-related problems for air traffic are usually cleared up fairly quickly and airports are closed generally for no more than 24 hours. Puerto Rico was especially hard hit with serious flooding.
Airlines and forwarders that serve the Caribbean and Latin America are experienced in working around the storms. The hurricane season lasts through to around end-November.
"We expect traffic northbound from Puerto Rico to be light for a few days because of flooding and other hurricane related problems," said the executive of one all-cargo airline.
"There is always some place in the world we are having weather delays," said a spokesman for Federal Express Corp., "our systems are designed to cope with this."
FedEx added extra flights last Wednesday to Puerto Rico and the Caribbean to bring down backlogs and will deliver packages as the flooding allows.

The hurricane season coincides with some of the busiest months for Miami freight. Forwarders and airline executives said that business is already beginning to pick up for the busy winter season after the lighter summer months.

November is usually Miami's busiest month, according to airport executives. The heavier winter cargo traffic is due partly to Latin American merchants stocking up for Christmas. Also more flowers, fruits and vegetables come northbound to the wintery United States and Europe.

"We project that during November and December, Miami will handle 150,000 tons of international cargo per month, approximately 10 percent to 15 percent above winter 1995," said Peter Reaveley, Miami's director of route development.
Reaveley said that imports from Chile and Colombia, which are mostly perishables, are expected to be strong.

Forwarders also said they are coping reasonably well with new cargo security requirements the Federal Aviation Administration imposed on them effective August 28. The new rules require more documents and tracking of cargo.

"It is a pain in the neck and it slows things down, but there are no serious delays," said one forwarder. "The adjustment has been pretty good." -Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 8982 Fax +44 171 542 5017
